evidence.supportingExcerpt: The limit of blank describes an upper background response at a specified probability. A limit of detection concerns an amount that can be detected under stated false-call and detection-probability conditions; LoD95 specifies 95 per cent detection in the tested workflow. It is not a line above which every repeat must be positive, nor 95 per cent certainty that a person has disease. A limit of quantitation requires stated quantitative accuracy, including bias and imprecision goals. The limits answer different questions and have no universal spacing; they may coincide under a particular method and its criteria.

Evaluate repeated blanks and low-level specimens across the conditions the claim covers. Each finite set of repeats needs representative clinical specimens or suitably equivalent reference inputs. Record the analyte, amount or concentration units, specimen matrix, input, workflow boundary, assay version and acceptable false-positive, false-negative and quantitative-error rates. Matrix means the material surrounding the analyte; reference material with a known added analyte amount needs justified equivalence to the clinical specimen. A limit measured on purified material is not automatically a collection-to-report limit. Contamination, nonspecific signal, calibration bias, poor recovery, unrepresentative targets, different lots or operators and inadequate input can change performance. Calibration-slope sensitivity, analytical detection capability and clinical sensitivity are different uses of the same word.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: “We did not find it” needs a description of where and how we looked. A literature search can establish that no relevant publication was found within its queries, synonyms, databases, access and cutoff date; it cannot substitute for a biological experiment. Its population, comparator, endpoint, effect scale, uncertainty, follow-up and missing-data rules determine what remains open.

A literature search can establish that no relevant publication was found within its queries, synonyms, databases, access and cutoff date; it cannot substitute for a biological experiment. A negative assay means no signal met the detection rule in the tested preparation. Its interpretation depends on the material, recovery, units, controls, sensitivity, threshold, time and compartment sampled. A false negative occurs when the condition is present but the test says otherwise. A study missing a significance threshold asks a third question: whether the data met that analysis's decision rule. Its population, comparator, endpoint, effect scale, uncertainty, follow-up and missing-data rules determine what remains open.

canonicalTeaching.requirement: Nonsignificance does not establish no effect. A wide interval can leave important benefit and harm unresolved; the later-only event-information/power clause stays distinct from the original version.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Read the effect estimate and confidence interval together. Too few events can leave a study with low power and an interval compatible with meaningful benefit and harm. Precision concerns sampling uncertainty under the analysis; it does not remove bias. Evidence excluding a large effect need not exclude a smaller one, and an unresolved effect is neither evidence of benefit nor proof of exactly zero effect. Equivalence testing asks whether an effect lies within justified lower and upper bounds, preferably specified before seeing results, using an appropriate analysis. Non-inferiority instead asks whether a treatment is worse than its comparator by more than a prespecified margin. Neither question is settled by failing to reject a zero difference, and meaningful margins depend on the outcome and setting.

Even a narrower interval would need a sound design, justified prespecified bounds and the appropriate analysis. These numbers are not a patient estimate.
